result.title: Preface
result.summary: The document is INPRS’s Request for Proposals No. 22-04 for Core Plus Fixed Income Investment Management, released October 31, 2022. Inquiries were due November 18 and proposals December 23, 2022, both by 3:00 p.m. EST. It covers the RFP introduction, INPRS background, issuer and contacts, inquiry and submission procedures, offer changes or withdrawal, confidentiality, response costs, proposal validity, taxes, registration, discussions, compliance certification, and milestones. Proposal requirements include general instructions, a transmittal letter, business proposal, and fee proposal. Further sections describe the scope of services and contract award, including contract term and evaluation criteria. Appendices provide essential clauses and a sample investment management agreement, mandatory taxpayer identification and foreign registration forms, and a questionnaire.

result.title: SECTION 1 – INTRODUCTION
result.summary: INPRS seeks qualified firms to manage its strategic Core Plus Fixed Income allocation. The section describes INPRS’s statutory status, administration of 16 funds, approximately $42.5 billion in assets, defined-benefit return assumption, investment allocation targets and defined-contribution options. It identifies INPRS as issuer and Capital Cities as the assisting consultant. Respondents must use the designated inquiry process; proposals were due December 23, 2022, and could be changed or withdrawn before the deadline. INPRS may issue addenda, extend deadlines, allow correction of minor omissions, or disqualify responses for major omissions or unauthorized contact. Proposal records are generally public, with procedures for claiming confidentiality and submitting redacted copies. Respondents bear their costs, must maintain proposal validity, and cannot charge INPRS taxes. Out-of-state corporations must register before contract discussions. INPRS may hold discussions and seek clarification. Respondents certify compliance with state obligations and must report new actions; INPRS may investigate and impose remedies. The section concludes with solicitation milestones through selection and contract negotiation.

nodes.summary:
SECTION 1 – INTRODUCTION
1.1 Title
Request for Proposals (“RFP”) for core plus fixed income investment management services for the Indiana Public Retirement System (“INPRS” or the “System”)
1.2 Overview of Request for Core Plus Fixed Income Investment Management
INPRS is soliciting proposals from all qualified investment firms who wish to be considered as an investment manager to provide portfolio management services for INPRS’ strategic allocation to Core Plus Fixed Income.

nodes.title: 1.3 INPRS Background
key_items: 1.1 Title; 1.2 Overview of Request for Core Plus Fixed Income Investment Management
1.2 Overview of Request for Core Plus Fixed Income Investment Management
nodes.summary: Established by 2011 statute, INPRS is an independent body corporate and governmental instrumentality—not a state department or agency—that administers 16 funds for Indiana public employees: eight defined benefit funds (PERF DB; TRF Pre-’96 DB and ’96 DB; ’77 Fund; JRS; EG&C; PARF; LE DB), five defined contribution funds (PERF DC and My Choice; TRF DC and My Choice; LE DC), two OPEB funds (SDBF and RMBA), and the custodial LPSPR. INPRS manages about $42.5 billion; its defined benefit plan assumes a 6.25% investment return. Portfolio target allocations (ranges) are public equity 20% (17–23%), private markets 15% (10–20%), non-inflation-linked fixed income 20% (17–23%), inflation-linked fixed income 15% (12–18%), commodities 10% (7–13%), real assets 10% (5–15%), absolute return 5% (0–10%), and risk parity 20% (15–25%); total exposure is 115%, maximum 120%. The DC plan has seven core options and target-date funds totaling about $6 billion. The text provides links to INPRS information, annual reports, and DC investment fact sheets.

nodes.title: 1.4 Issuer

1.4 Issuer
INPRS is issuing this RFP in accordance with Indiana statutes governing the procurement of services and certain administrative policies of INPRS. Capital Cities is INPRS’s defined contribution consulting firm and assisted INPRS staff in the preparation of this RFP and will consult on the evaluation of responses.

nodes.title: 1.5 Contacts
nodes.summary: Respondents must direct inquiries only through the RFP process; unauthorized contact with INPRS staff or trustees may disqualify them. Questions must be emailed to procurement contact Stanton Lanman by the deadlines in Section 1.16; INPRS may answer in writing and post responses, revisions, or interpretations as website addenda, potentially extending the proposal deadline. Proposals were due by email on December 23, 2022, at 3:00 p.m. EST; late submissions will not be considered. Offers may be modified or withdrawn in writing before the deadline. INPRS may allow all affected respondents five calendar days to correct minor errors or omissions after notice; major omissions, including missing prices, may lead to disqualification. Proposal materials are subject to Indiana’s Access to Public Records law; the excerpt ends before further details.

result.title: SECTION 2 – PROPOSAL CONTENT REQUIREMENTS
result.summary: The section establishes the required proposal format and electronic submission process. A complete submission must include a transmittal letter, business proposal, fee proposal, and Form W-9. The transmittal letter identifies the RFP and respondent, provides contact details, confirms capability and willingness to meet RFP and INPRS contract terms, and includes an authorized signature and proof of authority. Confidentiality claims must identify each protected item, its statutory basis and rationale, and include a redacted public version; blanket or incomplete claims are rejected. The business proposal must follow the specified headings and include an executive summary, experience and personnel details, organizational capability and financial statements/audit, a completed questionnaire, explained exceptions and proposed amendments to the base agreement (essential clauses are non-negotiable), and response assumptions, including INPRS responsibilities. The fee proposal must detail all costs in U.S. dollars based on Section 3 services and asset thresholds, remain guaranteed through the contract term, be paid quarterly in arrears, and answer the questionnaire’s fees and terms portion; inadequate detail may disqualify the respondent.

result.title: SECTION 3 – SCOPE OF SERVICES
result.summary: INPRS seeks proposals for two Core Plus Fixed Income managers for its DC Plan, with a combined mandate of about $185 million, benchmarked to the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index and governed by its Investment Policy Statement. The RFP aims to identify qualified firms with suitable expertise, performance history, and resources. Requirements include SEC registration; at least $2 billion firm AUM; 10 years managing Core Plus fixed income; at least seven years of GIPS-compliant strategy and senior-team performance; at least $500 million strategy AUM and $100 million capacity; and an active, long-only approach targeting benchmark-beating risk-adjusted returns net of fees. Firms must offer an eligible vehicle (separate accounts or collective trusts preferred) and comply with the IPS. Separate accounts require specified Sudan, terror-state, and Israel-related divestment screens and acceptance of INPRS contracts. The DC Fixed Income Fund is split equally between passive Aggregate exposure and two Core Plus managers; it also supports the Target Date glidepath. INPRS may leverage DB assets and manager relationships, with BNY Mellon unitizing mandates and fees negotiated across plans.

result.title: SECTION 4 – CONTRACT AWARD
result.summary: INPRS may award to the proposal(s) most advantageous under all evaluation factors, take other action or make no award, and, if a selected contract cannot be completed, negotiate with the next qualified respondent or decline to award. INPRS may clarify proposals, reject any or all, award without discussions, and divide the investment contract among multiple respondents; proposals should therefore offer best price and technical terms. The Executive Director or designee makes the final discretionary selection. The contract runs five years from execution, with optional renewals on the same terms, for a maximum total of ten years. A qualified evaluation team assesses proposals for ability to meet requirements efficiently and cost-effectively, with quality service and minimal error, and may consider other material factors. Criteria include performance (returns and tracking error on comparable core-plus fixed-income mandates), investment process, organizational ownership and strategy, investment-team integrity, depth, experience and stability, risk management, public-plan experience, fees, and portfolio characteristics.

result.title: APPENDIX A – SAMPLE INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT
result.summary: Appendix A provides the sample investment management agreement to be used if an award is made. Respondents should review it and submit proposed amendments with their business proposal, following RFP section 2.3.6, explaining each change and stating whether it is required or merely desired. INPRS is unlikely to accept changes unless, in its discretion, they are necessary to perform the services. If a required change is unacceptable, the proposal may be rejected; Appendix A.1 lists non-negotiable essential clauses. Respondents must clearly identify and explain all exceptions to the solicitation’s terms and conditions. Exceptions may negatively affect evaluation, and INPRS may refuse to consider exceptions not disclosed in the proposal.

result.title: APPENDIX A.1 – ESSENTIAL CLAUSES
result.summary: Appendix A.1 identifies mandatory, non-negotiable contract clauses and prohibited terms, including limits on indemnity, liability, governing law, venue, dispute resolution, taxes, fees, advance payment, records, disclosure, ethics, nondiscrimination, audits, and subcontracting. It includes a bidder acknowledgment and a template INPRS investment-management agreement covering term, definitions, appointment, fiduciary duties, instructions, custody, trading, reporting, meetings, compensation, termination, indemnification, representations, insurance, recordkeeping, confidentiality, conflicts, legal and ethics compliance, disputes, notices, funding, interpretation, entire agreement, severability, waivers, assignment, drug-free workplace, audits, authority, debarment, MBE/WBE requirements, non-collusion, and signatures. Exhibits address the mandate and benchmark, fee schedule and comparable-investor fee protections, prohibited brokers, authorized persons, the investment policy statement, and placement-agent disclosures.

nodes.title: Essential Clauses in the System’s Investment Management Agreement
nodes.summary: RFP respondents must review and comment on the System’s boilerplate investment management agreement; listed clauses are non-negotiable, and bids should account for any liability risks. Section 17 preserves the Manager’s indemnification duties and the System’s ability to recover damages; the System cannot indemnify the Manager. Section 18(H) investigations and complaints is essential and cannot be materially changed. Section 21 requires records retention under applicable law, including Indiana schedules, and inspection. Section 22 addresses confidential public records and required Social Security disclosures. Section 25 requires nondiscrimination without liability limits or substituted policies. Section 26(B) requires Indiana ethics compliance, including telephone solicitation rules. Section 28 mandates Indiana law and state-court venue, preserving Eleventh Amendment immunity. Section 29 rejects advance binding dispute resolution except Indiana courts, but permits later ADR. Sections 38 and 39 require unmodified drug-free workplace provisions and audit terms. Section 44 requires managers using subcontractors to offer bidding opportunities to listed Indiana-certified minority- or women-owned businesses; it does not apply without subcontractors.

nodes.title: 2. Definitions, Gender and Number
key_items: THIS INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT; A. Agents; B. Authorized Instructions; C. Authorized Persons
nodes.summary: The section establishes that capitalized terms have the stated meanings and that masculine, feminine, and neuter genders, and singular and plural forms, include one another unless context requires otherwise. It defines Agents as Manager’s service-providing employees, agents, or representatives, excluding independent providers; Authorized Instructions as directions from Authorized Persons, who are System-designated personnel authorized to direct Manager; and Board as the System’s Board of Trustees. Claims covers liabilities and related losses, expenses, proceedings, judgments, fines, and penalties connected with the agreement. It defines the Custodian and separate Sub-Account holding and accounting for Managed Assets; the Disclosure Statement as Manager’s SEC Form ADV Part II; and the Effective Termination Date as the cessation date in the System’s notice. Investment Guidelines comprise the IPS and agreement scope; Legal Requirements include applicable laws and regulatory requirements. Managed Assets include allocated System property and all related additions and growth. Standard of Care requires expert fiduciary care, skill, prudence, and diligence. System Records include all relevant records created or maintained by Manager or its Agents.

nodes.title: 3. Appointment of Manager and Acceptance of Appointment
nodes.summary: The System appoints the Manager as fiduciary to invest and manage the Managed Assets under the mandate and benchmark specified in Exhibit A; the Manager accepts responsibility and agrees to follow the Agreement. The Manager and its agents must meet the defined Standard of Care, and the Manager is liable for related claims arising from failures. The Manager acts only as the System’s limited agent, not as its employee, partner, or joint venturer; service providers are the Manager’s employees. The System supplies and updates in writing a list of Authorized Persons and signature specimens (Exhibit D); absent a designee, the Manager takes direction from the Executive Director. Authorized Instructions must generally be written and authenticated, though verbal instructions may be accepted with written confirmation. Unauthorized instructions must be rejected and reported; in exceptional circumstances, the Manager may sell securities to prevent exceptional loss when authorized persons cannot be reached. The System’s Custodian maintains a separate Sub-Account; the System retains ownership, and the Manager may not take possession, custody, title, or ownership of the assets.

nodes.title: Manager Duties, Agency, and Authorized Instructions
nodes.summary: The benchmark is determined under Exhibit A. The Manager owes the System and its agents the defined fiduciary Standard of Care and is liable for related claims arising from failures to meet it. The Manager acts solely as agent for managing the Managed Assets; the agreement creates no employment, partnership, joint venture, or similar relationship, and service providers are employees only of the Manager. The System supplies and updates in writing a list of Authorized Persons and applicable signature specimens; until notified of changes, the Manager may rely on the current list. If none is designated, the Manager takes direction only from the Executive Director. Authorized Instructions must be written and sent by specified mail, courier, fax, or authenticated electronic means, though verbal instructions may be accepted at the Manager’s discretion with written confirmation. Instructions bind upon receipt. The Manager must reject and report unauthorized instructions to the Chief Investment Officer, but may exercise discretion to dispose of securities in extraordinary circumstances when an Authorized Person cannot be reached, to prevent exceptional loss of value.

nodes.title: 8. Custody of Managed Assets
key_items: 4. Standard of Care; 5. Limited Status as Agent; 6. Authorized System Personnel
nodes.summary: The System must direct its Custodian to maintain a separate Sub-Account that tracks Managed Assets and related transactions apart from the System’s other assets. The System retains ownership. The Manager may not possess or hold custody, title, or ownership of the assets; register securities in its or a nominee’s name; or acquire income or proceeds from them. The Manager has no responsibility for collecting income, physically acquiring, or safeguarding the assets; those duties belong solely to the Custodian.

nodes.title: 9. Investment Duties of Manager
key_items: A. Investment Guidelines; B. Trading Procedures; C. Broker/Dealers
nodes.summary: The Manager, as fiduciary, may manage the Sub-Account under the agreement, IPS, Investment Guidelines, and applicable law. It may trade subject to the Guidelines and written revisions received from the System. Trades settle through the System’s Custodian, which retains the assets; the Manager directs trades and supplies settlement information. The Manager must prudently select reputable brokers for favorable net execution, avoid brokers barred by the System or affiliated with the investment consultant or Manager, and follow notified list changes. It must send confirmations to the Custodian, use DTC’s Institutional Delivery System when eligible, and help resolve settlement issues. The Board and Authorized Persons must forward information on asset rights and keep securities deliverable; the Manager directs timely action on rights it knows of. The Custodian provides requested online access and statements, and the Manager cooperates in monthly reconciliation without guaranteeing supplied information’s accuracy. Reports use agreed formats, trade-date accounting and accruals where available, and are signed and certified. Monthly reports cover performance, portfolio characteristics versus benchmarks, sector/country weights, and performance attributes; requested regulatory statements and filings are due within 30 days. Meetings occur upon request at mutually agreed times.

nodes.title: Managed Account Operations, Reconciliation, and Reporting
nodes.summary: The Manager uses the Company’s Institutional Delivery System for trade confirmation and settlement and cooperates to resolve settlement discrepancies. The Board or Authorized Persons must promptly pass along Custodian information about rights or events requiring investment decisions and ensure securities are held in deliverable form. The Manager directs action on such rights when it has actual knowledge. On request and where possible, the Custodian provides online Sub-Account access and reasonably requested statements; the Manager disclaims responsibility for the accuracy of information supplied by the System or Custodian but cooperates in monthly reconciliation. Reports use mutually agreed formats, trade-date accounting, and accrual treatment for income where available. An authorized officer signs and certifies them as accurate and consistent with Investment Guidelines; the Manager disclaims responsibility for third-party information. By month-end, the Manager reports the prior month’s investment status and performance, including benchmark comparisons, sector and country weights, and performance attributes. Within 30 days of request, it provides regulatory statements, responses, and filings concerning relevant financial or regulatory matters.

nodes.title: 12. Meetings
key_items: E. Discretionary Rights and Powers Affecting the Managed Assets
nodes.summary: The System may request mutually scheduled meetings to review the Manager’s performance and investment strategy; the Manager must also answer System staff and Board questions on reasonable notice at no extra charge. Compensation is mutually agreed, initially under Exhibit B’s fee schedule. The Manager must use required invoice forms and submit quarterly invoices within 30 days after each quarter, covering only services already performed, with partial quarters prorated; payments are made in arrears under Indiana law and System policies. Subject to applicable ethics rules, the System may attend the Manager’s client seminars and training on the same terms. The System may terminate the agreement, in whole or in part, for any reason by notice. The Manager retains System records under the agreement’s retention provisions and is paid for services through the effective termination date. A final invoice, daily-prorated at the current fee rate, is due within 30 days; if late, the System determines any amount due based on available information, and that determination is final. The System then authorizes payment and is not liable for post-termination services.

nodes.title: Manager Services, Compensation, and Training
nodes.summary: The Manager will review performance and investment strategy with the System and, on reasonable notice, answer System staff and Board members’ questions without extra charge. Compensation is mutually agreed, initially under Exhibit B’s fee schedule, and covers all services. The Manager must submit required forms and quarterly invoices within 30 days after each quarter, including prorated fees for partial quarters. Invoices may cover only completed services; payment is made in arrears under Indiana law and System policies. Subject to applicable state and System ethics rules, the System may attend the Manager’s client seminars and training events on the same terms as other clients.

nodes.title: 16. Termination; Rights, Remedies, and Responsibilities upon Termination; Termination for Convenience
nodes.summary: The System may terminate the agreement in whole or part for any reason by notice, or immediately if it considers termination necessary to protect the plan or trust assets. The Manager must retain System Records and is entitled to payment for services rendered before the effective termination date, subject to the contract price plus written-approved changes. Within 30 days, it must submit a reasonably certified final invoice prorating unpaid quarterly fees daily at its current compensation level; if it fails, the System’s estimate based on available information is final. The System then authorizes payment and is not liable for post-termination services. Termination does not waive claims for either party’s earlier defaults. Unless directed otherwise, the Manager must stop services on the effective date, but continue necessary work on pending transactions during a transition period of up to three months, at the existing compensation level, and cooperate in transferring services and records to a successor. Remedies under this section are cumulative and nonexclusive.

nodes.title: 17. Indemnification
nodes.summary:
17. Indemnification
Manager shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless the State of Indiana and the System, its officers, fiduciaries (excluding Manager), employees, and agents, from and against any and all Claims arising from or relating to any bad faith, negligence, willful misconduct, improper or unethical practice, infringement of intellectual property rights, breach of fiduciary duty, breach of trust, breach of confidentiality, breach of Agreement, violation of any Legal Requirement, or any other act or omission of or by Manager or any of its Agents acting in connection with this Management Agreement. This indemnification shall survive any termination of this Management Agreement. The System shall not provide such indemnification to Manager.

nodes.title: 18. Manager’s Representations, Warranties, and Covenants
nodes.summary: The Manager represents that it is authorized to enter and perform the agreement, which is binding subject to insolvency and equity limitations, and that performance violates no law, order, or agreement. It must meet service standards, promptly correct requested errors or omissions, avoid knowingly infringing intellectual-property rights or using trade secrets, and provide its auditor’s opinion letter and ADV Part II annually. It warrants compliance with restrictions on contingent-fee solicitors (subject to stated exceptions) and gratuities; breaches may result in termination and fee recovery or deduction, with gratuity violations permitting termination on one calendar day’s written notice. Within three business days it must report specified material changes, including inaccurate representations, personnel, control, organizational or portfolio-management changes, and bankruptcy filings. It must promptly report specified investigations, examinations, complaints, and proceedings, with information kept confidential until public unless law requires otherwise. The Manager also represents its investment-adviser registration (or exemption), ERISA Section 3(38) status, asset status, responsible agents’ qualifications and disciplinary history, disclosed placement-agent fees, and delivery of its Disclosure Statement; it acknowledges the System’s reliance on these commitments.

nodes.title: 18. Manager’s Representations, Warranties, and Covenants (intro)
nodes.summary: Manager represents that it is authorized to enter and perform the agreement, which is binding subject to standard insolvency and equity limitations, and that doing so violates no law, order, or agreement. Services must meet contractual standards, and Manager must promptly correct errors or omissions on request. Manager warrants it has not used prohibited contingent-fee solicitors; breach permits immediate termination for default and recovery or deduction of the fee. nodes.summary: Manager must provide and maintain insurance throughout the agreement to protect the System and Indiana from claims arising from negligent or intentional acts or omissions by Manager, subcontractors, or their agents. Fidelity coverage must be at least $3 million per occurrence and aggregate, covering employee dishonesty, physical loss or disappearance of property, forged instruments, and computer manipulation. nodes.title: I. BACKGROUND & GENERAL INFORMATION
nodes.summary: A due-diligence questionnaire for Core Plus fixed-income managers covering firm and primary-contact details; history, affiliates, investment focus, corporate strategy, growth targets, and planned products; organizational and ownership changes; other business lines and their revenue/AUM; investment platform, product lineup, mandate-level AUM, and fixed-income assets by style over time, including material flows. It asks about Core Plus clients and investor mix, staffing, research, clients, and firm-wide AUM over ten years; office locations, functions, and team locations; significant and employee ownership, convertible or revenue-linked debt, subsidiaries, joint ventures, and financial arrangements. It also addresses broker-dealer affiliations, client trading, soft dollars, personnel management, product-group profit sharing, succession and continuity, terminated strategies or products, and women- and minority-ownership status.

nodes.title: II. INVESTMENT TEAM
nodes.summary: The section requests details on the investment team managing the proposed mandate: groups, responsibilities, functional organization, decision-makers, and employee counts, gains, and losses by role for the prior three calendar years and YTD through June 30, 2022. It asks about key individuals’ other duties, time allocated to the mandate, and other-strategy AUM; formal committees’ purpose, participants, frequency, and decision/override authority; and investment-professional compensation, bonus criteria, contracts, and retention arrangements. It also covers individuals’ personal investments in the mandate and any favorable commingled-fund terms, succession and continuity plans, talent-development and hiring preferences, views on specialist versus generalist analysts and portfolio managers, material team-structure changes and their timing and reasons, and any outsourced investment activities, providers’ roles, and affiliate status.

nodes.title: III. INVESTMENT STRATEGY
nodes.summary: The questionnaire seeks details on the Core Plus strategy’s investment philosophy, active-management value, process and evolution, including top-down/bottom-up research, competitive advantages, quantitative and qualitative decisions, portfolio constraints, and ESG use and policy. It covers investment-thesis and security analysis, sell discipline, position sizing and portfolio breadth, non-benchmark securities, derivatives, currency exposure and hedging, and changes in the fixed-income universe. It asks how process compliance and periodic reviews are handled, including material changes. Other topics include technology, portfolio and operational tools and planned enhancements; trading capabilities across markets and time zones; mandate and firm asset growth; expected performance in different environments and lessons from strong and weak periods; and performance attribution methods and their use. Requested supporting information includes current portfolio characteristics, historical subsector exposures, and independently verified GIPS-compliant Core Plus composite performance and verification, or an explanation if unavailable.

nodes.title: IV. RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.summary: The section asks how risk is defined for the mandate, whether a tracking-error target or risk budget is used, and how portfolio risk is allocated across countries, currencies, duration, and securities, both absolutely and relative to the benchmark. It requests details of risk monitoring functions and tools, including responsible individuals and contacts; key non-investment risks and controls to mitigate them; and how risk management collaborates with, yet remains independent of, other investment functions. It also covers escalation when risk metrics breach targets, mandate counterparties and transaction types, counterparty-risk monitoring and management, material changes to risk and portfolio-monitoring processes with their timing and reasons, and safeguards for compliance with investment guidelines.

It also asks about outside ownership, economic arrangements, affiliations, and affiliated-firm compensation, including services, fees, and payment sources; employee personal-trading policies; family relationships among operations or compliance staff and conflict safeguards; other mandate-related conflicts and controls; professional counterparties and relationship duration (legal advisers, auditors, banks, marketers, administrators, prime brokers, and others); and operational-risk management, SSAE 18 or equivalent reviews, and available auditor opinions on control design and effectiveness.
